Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- The economic downturn may take its toll at the 2009 Cannes Film Festival, which opens Wednesday night. But as always, the show will go on. Eli Roth and Brad Pitt are men on a mission in Quentin Tarantino's "Inglourious Basterds." Studios are cutting back on parties and all the glitz that goes with them, according to news reports. Moreover, there will be fewer people around to cover Cannes, as news organizations around the world trim costs. (Several, in fact, have tightened up by eliminating their movie reviewers.) Nevertheless, those who attend may see a bumper crop of good and intriguing films, Variety's Jay Weissberg told Reuters. "We've all been hoping Cannes would pull something out of the bag to make us feel good again. On paper, they have." Leah Rozen, film critic for People magazine, said there are several promising contenders for the Palme d'Or, Cannes' top prize, as well as a number of notable movies premiering out of competition. "What Cannes really is, is an international festival, and you really see world cinema," she said. "This year, there are 52 films that are going to be represented, of which 20 are in competition."  See Rozen talk about some of this year's promising works » . Two of the films in competition are American: Quentin Tarantino's World War II movie, "Inglourious Basterds," and Ang Lee's "Taking Woodstock," a tale about the 1969 music festival. Tarantino told The New York Times that he's been hoping to do a war movie for years. "You've got to make a movie about something, and I'm a film guy, so I think in terms of genres," he said. However, the maker of "Pulp Fiction" and "Jackie Brown" added, that doesn't mean what he ends up with resembles what he started with: "It's simply the spark that starts the fire." "Inglourious Basterds" was inspired by a 1978 Italian film that starred Bo Svenson ("Walking Tall, Part 2") and football player-turned-actor Fred Williamson ("Black Caesar"). Tarantino's film, which he characterized to the Times as "not a remake," stars Brad Pitt and Mike Myers. Cannes has been good to Tarantino; he won the Palme d'Or for "Pulp Fiction" 15 years ago. Buzz has been high on "Basterds" since Tarantino announced the project several years ago. "Taking Woodstock," the new film by "Brokeback Mountain" director Lee, is based on the book by Elliot Tiber, whose hotelier parents owned a musical festival permit in Bethel, New York, where Woodstock was held. The cast includes Liev Schreiber, Jeffrey Dean Morgan, Emile Hirsch, Imelda Staunton and Eugene Levy as Max Yasgur, on whose farm the festival was finally held. Other films in competition include Lars von Trier's "Antichrist," Jane Campion's "Bright Star" and Pedro Almodovar's "Broken Embraces."  Gallery: Some of Cannes' recent winners » . But this year's Cannes festival is attracting plenty of attention for its out-of-competition films as well. The festival is opening with "Up," the latest animated work from Pixar. "That sort of breaks convention to open with what is, basically, a fancy cartoon," Rozen said. Also at Cannes will be Heath Ledger's last film, "The Imaginarium of Dr. Parnassus." The Oscar-winning "Dark Knight" actor died during the making of the Terry Gilliam film; Gilliam managed to complete it by doing some rewriting and casting other actors -- including Jude Law, Colin Farrell and Johnny Depp -- to play Ledger's part. Despite the interest in seeing Ledger, the film is still struggling to find a buyer, though Entertainment Weekly recently reported that a Los Angeles screening went over well. Cannes, which also functions as a huge film marketplace, may widen the net in attracting distributors. But much of the fun from Cannes comes from the films that emerge from nowhere. Recent winners of the Palme d'Or include 2000's "Dancer in the Dark," which established singer Bjork as an actress, and "4 Months, 3 Weeks and 2 Days," a Romanian film that ended up topping many critics' lists in 2007. "One thing that always surprises me is that some of the films you have the lowest expectations for turn out to be terrific, and sometimes the bigger films turn out to be disappointments," Rozen said.

(CNN) — The economic downturn may cast a shadow over the 2009 Cannes Film Festival, which opens Wednesday night. But, as always, the show will go on.

Eli Roth and Brad Pitt are men on a mission in Quentin Tarantino’s “Inglourious Basterds.”

According to news reports, studios are scaling back on parties and the accompanying glamour. In addition, fewer people are expected to be on hand to cover Cannes, as news organizations around the world cut costs. Several, in fact, have tightened their budgets by eliminating movie reviewers.

Nevertheless, those who attend may be rewarded with a bumper crop of strong and intriguing films, Variety’s Jay Weissberg told Reuters.

“We’ve all been hoping Cannes would pull something out of the bag to make us feel good again. On paper, they have.”

Leah Rozen, film critic for People magazine, said there are several promising contenders for the Palme d’Or, Cannes’ top prize, as well as a number of notable movies premiering out of competition.

“What Cannes really is, is an international festival, and you really see world cinema,” she said. “This year, there are 52 films that are going to be represented, of which 20 are in competition.”

See Rozen talk about some of this year’s promising works »

Two of the films in competition are American: Quentin Tarantino’s World War II movie, “Inglourious Basterds,” and Ang Lee’s “Taking Woodstock,” a tale about the 1969 music festival.

Tarantino told The New York Times that he had hoped for years to make a war movie.

“You’ve got to make a movie about something, and I’m a film guy, so I think in terms of genres,” he said.

However, the maker of “Pulp Fiction” and “Jackie Brown” added that this does not mean the finished work resembles the idea with which he began: “It’s simply the spark that starts the fire.”

“Inglourious Basterds” was inspired by a 1978 Italian film starring Bo Svenson, of “Walking Tall, Part 2,” and football player-turned-actor Fred Williamson, of “Black Caesar.” Tarantino’s film, which he characterized to the Times as “not a remake,” stars Brad Pitt and Mike Myers.

Cannes has been good to Tarantino; he won the Palme d’Or for “Pulp Fiction” 15 years ago. Anticipation for “Basterds” has been high since Tarantino announced the project several years ago.

“Taking Woodstock,” the new film by “Brokeback Mountain” director Lee, is based on the book by Elliot Tiber, whose hotelier parents owned a music festival permit in Bethel, New York, where Woodstock was held. The cast includes Liev Schreiber, Jeffrey Dean Morgan, Emile Hirsch, Imelda Staunton and Eugene Levy as Max Yasgur, on whose farm the festival ultimately took place.

Other films in competition include Lars von Trier’s “Antichrist,” Jane Campion’s “Bright Star” and Pedro Almodóvar’s “Broken Embraces.”

Gallery: Some of Cannes’ recent winners »

This year’s Cannes festival, however, is also drawing considerable attention for its out-of-competition films. The festival opens with “Up,” the latest animated feature from Pixar.

“That sort of breaks convention to open with what is, basically, a fancy cartoon,” Rozen said.

Also at Cannes will be Heath Ledger’s final film, “The Imaginarium of Dr. Parnassus.” The Oscar-winning “Dark Knight” actor died during the making of the Terry Gilliam film. Gilliam managed to complete it through some rewriting and by casting other actors — including Jude Law, Colin Farrell and Johnny Depp — to play Ledger’s part.

Despite interest in seeing Ledger, the film is still struggling to find a buyer, though Entertainment Weekly recently reported that a Los Angeles screening was well received. Cannes, which also serves as a major film marketplace, may help broaden the search for distributors.

“One thing that always surprises me is that some of the films you have the lowest expectations for turn out to be terrific, and sometimes the bigger films turn out to be disappointments,” Rozen said.

(CNN) — The 2009 Cannes Film Festival, which begins Wednesday evening, could feel the effects of the global financial slump. Even so, the festival is expected to continue as usual.

In Quentin Tarantino’s “Inglourious Basterds,” Eli Roth and Brad Pitt play men with a mission. According to news accounts, studios are scaling down their celebrations and reducing the glamour that typically surrounds them. Fewer journalists are also expected to be present, as media companies worldwide cut expenses. Some outlets have even saved money by dropping their film critics.

Still, Variety critic Jay Weissberg told Reuters that festivalgoers may be treated to an unusually strong and interesting lineup. “We’ve all been hoping Cannes would pull something out of the bag to make us feel good again. On paper, they have.”

People magazine film critic Leah Rozen said the competition for the Palme d’Or, Cannes’ highest honor, includes several strong possibilities, while the festival also features many noteworthy premieres outside the main competition.

“What Cannes really is, is an international festival, and you really see world cinema,” Rozen said. “This year, there are 52 films that are going to be represented, of which 20 are in competition.”

Two of the movies competing for the Palme d’Or are from the United States: Tarantino’s World War II film “Inglourious Basterds” and Ang Lee’s “Taking Woodstock,” which tells a story connected to the 1969 music festival.

Tarantino told The New York Times that he had long wanted to make a war film. “You’ve got to make a movie about something, and I’m a film guy, so I think in terms of genres,” he said. But the director of “Pulp Fiction” and “Jackie Brown” noted that the final result does not necessarily match the original idea. “It’s simply the spark that starts the fire.”

“Inglourious Basterds” was influenced by a 1978 Italian movie featuring Bo Svenson of “Walking Tall, Part 2” and former football player-turned-actor Fred Williamson of “Black Caesar.” Tarantino told the Times that his version is “not a remake.” His film stars Brad Pitt and Mike Myers.

Cannes has been a significant place in Tarantino’s career: 15 years earlier, he received the Palme d’Or for “Pulp Fiction.” Anticipation surrounding “Basterds” has been strong since he first revealed the project several years ago.

“Taking Woodstock,” the latest movie from “Brokeback Mountain” director Ang Lee, is adapted from Elliot Tiber’s book. Tiber’s parents, who ran a hotel, possessed a music festival permit in Bethel, New York, the town where Woodstock took place. The cast features Liev Schreiber, Jeffrey Dean Morgan, Emile Hirsch, Imelda Staunton and Eugene Levy, who plays Max Yasgur, the farmer whose land ultimately hosted the festival.

Other Palme d’Or contenders include Lars von Trier’s “Antichrist,” Jane Campion’s “Bright Star” and Pedro Almodóvar’s “Broken Embraces.”

This year’s Cannes is also drawing considerable interest for films showing outside the competition. The festival will begin with “Up,” Pixar’s newest animated feature. Rozen said that choice is unusual: “That sort of breaks convention to open with what is, basically, a fancy cartoon.”

Also screening at Cannes is “The Imaginarium of Dr. Parnassus,” the final film featuring Heath Ledger. The Oscar-winning star of “The Dark Knight” died while Terry Gilliam’s movie was still being made. Gilliam completed the project by revising parts of it and bringing in other actors, including Jude Law, Colin Farrell and Johnny Depp, to portray Ledger’s role.

Although Ledger’s final appearance has generated interest, the film had not yet secured a buyer. Entertainment Weekly recently reported, however, that a Los Angeles screening was well received. Because Cannes also serves as a major marketplace for films, the festival could help the movie reach more potential distributors.

A large part of Cannes’ appeal, though, lies in the unexpected discoveries. Recent Palme d’Or winners have included “Dancer in the Dark” from 2000, which helped establish singer Björk as an actress, and the Romanian drama “4 Months, 3 Weeks and 2 Days,” which went on to top many critics’ lists in 2007.

“One thing that always surprises me is that some of the films you have the lowest expectations for turn out to be terrific, and sometimes the bigger films turn out to be disappointments,” Rozen said.

**Cannes Film Festival opens under recession clouds, but star power remains**

*CANNES, France —* The red carpet is ready, the yachts are moored and the flashbulbs are waiting. But as the 62nd Cannes Film Festival prepares to open, even cinema’s most glamorous gathering is not immune to the global economic downturn.

This year’s festival arrives amid a recession that has squeezed film financing, trimmed corporate spending and cast uncertainty over the international sales market that runs alongside the premieres. Industry executives are expected to be watching budgets as closely as buzz, with fewer lavish parties and a more cautious mood among buyers.

Still, Cannes remains Cannes — and the 2009 lineup is packed with big-name filmmakers, anticipated premieres and the kind of star-driven spectacle that keeps the world’s attention fixed on the Croisette.

Among the most closely watched films in competition is **Quentin Tarantino’s “Inglourious Basterds,”** a World War II revenge saga starring Brad Pitt. Tarantino, a Cannes favorite since “Pulp Fiction” won the Palme d’Or in 1994, returns with one of the festival’s highest-profile entries.

Also competing for the Palme d’Or is **Ang Lee’s “Taking Woodstock,”** a 1960s-set comedy-drama about the birth of the legendary music festival. Lee, a two-time Oscar winner, brings a lighter touch to a competition slate that also includes works from acclaimed international directors such as Pedro Almodóvar, Lars von Trier, Ken Loach and Jane Campion.

The festival’s opening-night film, **“Up,”** marks a milestone for Cannes: the Pixar animated adventure is the first animated film to open the festival. Screening out of competition, the film is expected to bring a family-friendly burst of color to the Croisette.

Other notable out-of-competition premieres include **“The Imaginarium of Doctor Parnassus,”** Terry Gilliam’s fantasy film featuring Heath Ledger in his final screen performance. The movie was completed after Ledger’s death with help from Johnny Depp, Jude Law and Colin Farrell, making it one of the festival’s most talked-about screenings.

Cannes will also welcome major Hollywood fare, including **“Angels & Demons,”** the Ron Howard-directed follow-up to “The Da Vinci Code,” starring Tom Hanks, which is set for a high-profile showcase outside the main competition.

Despite the financial chill, festival organizers are expected to deliver the usual mix of prestige cinema, celebrity appearances and late-night dealmaking. For independent producers and international distributors, Cannes remains a crucial marketplace — even if the deals are smaller and the negotiations tougher this year.

By the time the Palme d’Or is awarded, the festival may offer a clearer snapshot of where the movie business stands in a battered global economy. But for now, Cannes is betting that, recession or not, the world still wants a little movie-star glamour.

Also drawing attention is Ang Lee’s **“Taking Woodstock,”** a period comedy-drama about the 1969 music festival and the cultural moment surrounding it. Lee, known for films ranging from **“Brokeback Mountain”** to **“Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon,”** brings a lighter, nostalgic entry to the competition lineup.

Another major premiere is **“The Imaginarium of Doctor Parnassus,”** directed by Terry Gilliam and notable as the final film appearance of **Heath Ledger**, who died in 2008 before production was completed. **Cannes 2009: Stars, auteurs and recession-era glamour on the Croisette**

*CANNES, France —* The red carpet will still be rolled out, the flashbulbs will still pop and the yachts will still crowd the harbor. But when the 62nd Cannes Film Festival opens, it will do so under the shadow of a global recession — and with a lineup that reminds the film world why Cannes remains the industry’s most prestigious stage.

This year’s festival, running May 13-24, is expected to mix Hollywood spectacle with the kind of provocative international cinema that has long defined the Croisette. Pixar’s animated adventure **“Up”** will open the festival — a rare animated kickoff and a reminder that Cannes, for all its auteur credentials, still knows how to make room for crowd-pleasing movie magic.

But the real intrigue lies in the race for the **Palme d’Or**, where an unusually strong field includes new films from Quentin Tarantino, Pedro Almodóvar, Jane Campion, Michael Haneke, Ken Loach, Lars von Trier and Jacques Audiard.

“This is one of those Cannes years where the competition feels like a roll call of modern cinema,” said London-based film critic **Martin Hale**. “You don’t come here just to see movies — you come to see which films are going to dominate the conversation for the next year.”

## A packed Palme d’Or race

Among the most anticipated premieres is **Quentin Tarantino’s “Inglourious Basterds,”** starring Brad Pitt in a World War II revenge fantasy that has been generating buzz for months. Tarantino won the Palme d’Or in 1994 for **“Pulp Fiction,”** and his return to competition is expected to be one of the festival’s biggest media events.

Spanish filmmaker **Pedro Almodóvar** returns with **“Broken Embraces,”** starring Penélope Cruz, while New Zealand director **Jane Campion** — the only woman to have won the Palme d’Or, for **“The Piano”** — is back in competition with **“Bright Star,”** a period romance about poet John Keats.

Austrian director **Michael Haneke**, long a Cannes favorite, brings **“The White Ribbon,”** a stark black-and-white drama set in a German village before World War I. French filmmaker **Jacques Audiard** arrives with **“A Prophet,”** a prison drama already viewed by many festival watchers as a major contender.

“Haneke and Audiard are the sort of filmmakers Cannes loves: rigorous, political, formally controlled,” said Paris critic **Claire Dubois**. “But Cannes also loves surprise. A film can arrive quietly and leave with the Palme.”

Other competition titles likely to spark debate include **Lars von Trier’s “Antichrist,”** starring Charlotte Gainsbourg and Willem Dafoe; **Ken Loach’s “Looking for Eric,”** a soccer-infused comedy-drama featuring Eric Cantona; **Park Chan-wook’s vampire film “Thirst”;** and **Gaspar Noé’s “Enter the Void,”** expected to deliver the kind of sensory overload that can either thrill or divide Cannes audiences.

The jury is headed by French actress **Isabelle Huppert**, herself a two-time Cannes acting prize winner. Her presence has added another layer of expectation: Huppert is known for challenging, uncompromising work, and many observers expect the jury to reward boldness over consensus.

## Glamour, but with a slimmer wallet

Still, this year’s Cannes will not be immune to the economic downturn. Across the film industry, budgets have tightened, and the festival is expected to feel slightly leaner than in boom years. Some companies are scaling back parties, promotional stunts and lavish beachfront events. Fewer private jets, smaller entourages and more cautious deal-making are likely to be part of the atmosphere.

“The champagne may be flowing a little less freely, but the business doesn’t stop,” said Los Angeles-based industry analyst **Rachel Kim**. “Cannes is where prestige, sales and global visibility meet. Even in a recession, that’s hard to replace.”

The film market running alongside the festival — the Marché du Film — remains one of the most important marketplaces in the world for international distribution. Producers, sales agents and buyers use Cannes to secure financing, sell territory rights and build awards-season momentum.

For independent filmmakers, the festival’s value can be enormous. A strong Cannes reception can transform a small art-house title into an international event. Critical acclaim on the Croisette can also provide a launchpad toward year-end awards consideration, especially for foreign-language films and prestige dramas.

## Why Cannes still matters

Part of Cannes’ staying power is its balance of contradictions. It is at once a luxury showcase and a serious cinematic institution; a celebrity magnet and a home for difficult, experimental work. Studios come for publicity, auteurs come for validation and critics come looking for the first great films of the year.

“Cannes is still the place where cinema declares its ambitions,” said critic **Hale**. “Toronto may be crucial for awards season, Sundance may define independent discovery, Venice may have history — but Cannes has the mythology.”

That mythology will be on display from the opening-night gala to the final awards ceremony. The festival’s out-of-competition slate and special screenings are also expected to draw attention, while the sidebar sections — including Un Certain Regard, Directors’ Fortnight and Critics’ Week — may produce some of the event’s most exciting discoveries.

Even with reduced spending, the essentials remain intact: world premieres, intense critical debate, late-night screenings, deal-making in hotel suites and the ritual of stars climbing the Palais steps beneath a wall of photographers.

“People always talk about Cannes glamour,” said Dubois. “But the real glamour is that a film can arrive unknown and, two hours later, become part of cinema history.”

## The films to watch

Key Palme d’Or contenders and high-profile competition titles include:

- **“Inglourious Basterds”** — Quentin Tarantino’s star-driven World War II epic  
- **“Broken Embraces”** — Pedro Almodóvar reunites with Penélope Cruz  
- **“Bright Star”** — Jane Campion’s romantic drama about John Keats  
- **“The White Ribbon”** — Michael Haneke’s austere prewar village mystery  
- **“A Prophet”** — Jacques Audiard’s gritty prison drama  
- **“Antichrist”** — Lars von Trier’s psychological horror film  
- **“Looking for Eric”** — Ken Loach’s football-themed crowd-pleaser  
- **“Thirst”** — Park Chan-wook’s vampire tale  
- **“Enter the Void”** — Gaspar Noé’s hallucinatory cinematic experiment  

As the global film industry navigates recession-era uncertainty, Cannes 2009 may be less extravagant around the edges. But on screen, the festival appears anything but diminished.

The parties may be smaller. The expense accounts may be tighter. The competition, however, looks fierce — and for Cannes, that is still what matters most.

# Cannes 2009 Festival Preview: Auteurs, Americans, Tarantino, Buzz Titles and the Business Behind the Glamour

The 62nd Cannes Film Festival, running May 13–24, 2009, arrives with one of the year’s most intriguing festival lineups: a mix of returning masters, politically charged international cinema, major American auteurs, art-house provocateurs, and a high-profile Hollywood presence on the Croisette. Presided over by jury president Isabelle Huppert, the 2009 edition looks designed to reaffirm Cannes’ dual identity: the world’s most prestigious showcase for cinema as art, and the most important annual marketplace for global film commerce.

This year’s Competition is especially heavy on established auteurs, with new work from Quentin Tarantino, Pedro Almodóvar, Michael Haneke, Jane Campion, Ken Loach, Alain Resnais, Lars von Trier, Park Chan-wook, Jacques Audiard and others. At the same time, Cannes 2009 is making room for American studio glamour, genre excitement, animated spectacle and the usual frisson of controversy.

---

## A Competition Lineup Built Around International Auteurs

Cannes’ main Competition in 2009 is unmistakably auteur-driven. The festival has assembled a slate that spans Europe, Asia, the Middle East, North America and Australia/New Zealand, with many filmmakers returning to familiar ground on the Riviera.

Among the most anticipated European entries is **Pedro Almodóvar’s “Broken Embraces”**, starring Penélope Cruz. Almodóvar is a Cannes regular, and his latest promises the director’s signature blend of melodrama, noir, romance and cinephilia. Coming after Cruz’s Oscar win for “Vicky Cristina Barcelona,” the film carries both art-house prestige and star power.

**Michael Haneke’s “The White Ribbon”** also arrives with significant expectations. Shot in stark black and white and set in a German village before World War I, the film is expected to offer Haneke’s usual clinical dissection of violence, repression and social control. Given Cannes’ long relationship with Haneke, the film is an immediate Palme d’Or contender on paper.

France is strongly represented. **Jacques Audiard’s “A Prophet”** is one of the most buzzed-about homegrown titles, a prison drama that could confirm Audiard’s status as one of contemporary French cinema’s major figures. Veteran master **Alain Resnais** returns with **“Wild Grass,”** while **Xavier Giannoli’s “In the Beginning”** adds another French-language title to the Competition.

The British presence is also notable. **Andrea Arnold’s “Fish Tank,”** following her acclaimed “Red Road,” brings social realism and young working-class drama to the Croisette. **Ken Loach**, one of Cannes’ most reliable political filmmakers, appears with **“Looking for Eric,”** a comedy-drama involving football culture and a fictionalized appearance by Eric Cantona.

From Italy, **Marco Bellocchio’s “Vincere”** dramatizes the story of Benito Mussolini’s first wife, suggesting a blend of historical drama, political critique and operatic intensity. Bellocchio is another Cannes veteran whose work fits comfortably into the festival’s tradition of politically engaged cinema.

Asian cinema has several major entries. South Korea’s **Park Chan-wook** brings **“Thirst,”** a vampire film that promises to mix genre, eroticism, religion and moral transgression in typical Park fashion. Hong Kong director **Johnnie To** enters with **“Vengeance,”** starring French rock icon Johnny Hallyday, combining international casting with To’s stylized crime-film expertise. Taiwanese master **Tsai Ming-liang** presents **“Face,”** a French-Taiwanese production that looks likely to be one of the more formally adventurous films in the program.

Chinese cinema is represented by **Lou Ye’s “Spring Fever,”** notable not only for its subject matter but also because Lou had faced official restrictions in China after “Summer Palace.” Its presence at Cannes underlines the festival’s continued role as a platform for filmmakers working under difficult political or cultural conditions.

The Middle East is represented by **Elia Suleiman’s “The Time That Remains,”** a personal and political work reflecting on Palestinian history and identity. Spanish filmmaker **Isabel Coixet** appears with **“Map of the Sounds of Tokyo,”** while the Philippines’ **Brillante Mendoza** brings **“Kinatay,”** expected to be one of the festival’s harsher and more divisive experiences.

And then there is **Lars von Trier’s “Antichrist,”** likely to be among the most talked-about films of the festival regardless of critical consensus. Starring Willem Dafoe and Charlotte Gainsbourg, the film has been trailed as a psychological horror piece involving grief, sexuality and violence. With von Trier, controversy is not a possibility so much as an expectation.

---

## American Entries in Competition: Tarantino and Ang Lee

The American presence in Competition is led by two very different filmmakers: **Quentin Tarantino** and **Ang Lee**.

### “Inglourious Basterds” — Quentin Tarantino  
Tarantino’s **“Inglourious Basterds”** is arguably the most eagerly awaited Competition title of Cannes 2009. A World War II revenge fantasy starring Brad Pitt, Mélanie Laurent, Christoph Waltz, Diane Kruger and Eli Roth, the film marks Tarantino’s return to the festival as a major event filmmaker.

The project has been discussed for years, and its Cannes berth gives the festival a shot of pop-cultural adrenaline. Tarantino has always been an intensely Cannes-friendly American director: internationalist, referential, cinephile, flamboyant and unafraid of genre. His new film is expected to merge war-movie iconography, pulp violence, multilingual dialogue and alternate-history audacity.

### “Taking Woodstock” — Ang Lee  
Ang Lee’s **“Taking Woodstock”** offers a different kind of American story. Set around the 1969 Woodstock festival, the film stars Demetri Martin, Imelda Staunton, Liev Schreiber and Emile Hirsch. Rather than a straight concert film, it appears to approach Woodstock through the story of those on the margins of the event, capturing the cultural mood and logistical chaos around a defining moment in countercultural history.

Lee is, of course, no stranger to Cannes or international acclaim. After films as varied as “The Ice Storm,” “Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon,” “Brokeback Mountain” and “Lust, Caution,” his presence in Competition gives Cannes another prestige American-linked title with broad international appeal.

Together, Tarantino and Lee provide Cannes 2009 with a useful contrast: one film promising revisionist genre bravado, the other period comedy-drama rooted in American cultural memory.

---

## Tarantino’s Return to Cannes

Quentin Tarantino’s relationship with Cannes is central to the mythology of his career. He won the Palme d’Or in 1994 for **“Pulp Fiction,”** a victory that helped reshape the international profile of American independent cinema and confirmed Cannes as a place where popular genre language could be treated as high art.

Since then, Tarantino has been both a Cannes favorite and a Cannes personality: part filmmaker, part fan, part showman. His return with **“Inglourious Basterds”** is one of the festival’s headline stories because it reconnects the director with the site of his greatest early triumph.

The question hovering over the film is whether Tarantino can once again convert cinephile enthusiasm into major festival recognition. Cannes has often rewarded boldness, but it can also be unpredictable with American genre-inflected cinema. Even if “Inglourious Basterds” does not win a top prize, it is certain to dominate red-carpet attention, press coverage and post-screening debate.

A key point of curiosity is tone. Will the film play as a war epic, a black comedy, a revenge fantasy, a movie-about-movies, or all of the above? The cast also adds to the fascination, particularly Brad Pitt as the leader of a Jewish-American commando unit and Christoph Waltz, relatively unknown to many international audiences before the film, in what early whispers suggest could be a standout role.

---

## Out-of-Competition Buzz: Hollywood, Animation, Genre and Spectacle

Cannes is not only about the Palme d’Or. The Out of Competition and special-screening slots often generate enormous attention, and 2009’s selections are designed to bring star power, mainstream curiosity and event cinema to the festival.

### “Up” Opens the Festival  
Pixar’s **“Up”** opens Cannes 2009, an especially notable choice because it marks the first time an animated feature has opened the festival. Directed by Pete Docter, the film brings a major American studio presence to the Croisette and signals Cannes’ willingness to treat animation as a premier cinematic event rather than a secondary category.

The opening-night slot is also significant because “Up” arrives in 3D, giving the festival a technologically modern curtain-raiser. For a festival sometimes associated with old-world glamour and art-house austerity, opening with Pixar is a bold acknowledgement of animation’s artistic and commercial power.

### “The Imaginarium of Doctor Parnassus”  
Terry Gilliam’s **“The Imaginarium of Doctor Parnassus”** is another major out-of-competition attraction. The film carries intense curiosity because it includes Heath Ledger’s final screen performance. After Ledger’s death, Johnny Depp, Jude Law and Colin Farrell stepped in to complete aspects of the role, giving the film an unusual behind-the-scenes story that will likely shape much of its Cannes reception.

Gilliam’s cinema is always visually extravagant and narratively eccentric, and Cannes offers an ideal platform for a film that may be difficult to categorize commercially but irresistible as a festival talking point.

### “Drag Me to Hell”  
Sam Raimi’s **“Drag Me to Hell”** brings genre energy to Cannes. Raimi’s return to horror after his “Spider-Man” years has been greeted with excitement by fans eager to see him reconnect with the anarchic spirit of “The Evil Dead.” Cannes has long had room for midnight-movie thrills alongside its more austere art cinema, and “Drag Me to Hell” should provide one of the festival’s more purely entertaining events.

### “Agora”  
Alejandro Amenábar’s **“Agora,”** starring Rachel Weisz, arrives as a large-scale historical drama about Hypatia of Alexandria. Its combination of intellectual history, religious conflict and epic production values makes it one of the more ambitious out-of-competition titles.

### Closing-Night Glamour  
The festival closes with **“Coco Chanel & Igor Stravinsky,”** Jan Kounen’s drama about the relationship between the fashion icon and the composer. It is an appropriately French, stylish and culturally branded finale for Cannes, combining fashion, music, romance and period spectacle.

---

## Themes to Watch: Politics, History, Violence and Cinephilia

The 2009 lineup suggests several recurring themes.

First, there is a strong engagement with history: World War II in “Inglourious Basterds,” prewar Germany in “The White Ribbon,” Mussolini-era Italy in “Vincere,” 1960s America in “Taking Woodstock,” and ancient Alexandria in “Agora.” Cannes 2009 appears preoccupied with the way private lives are shaped by ideological upheaval and collective memory.

Second, violence is everywhere, though in very different registers: Haneke’s moral severity, Tarantino’s stylized revenge, Park’s vampire horror, Mendoza’s brutality, von Trier’s psychological extremity and Audiard’s prison-world realism. This could be a Cannes defined by discomfort as much as glamour.

Third, cinephilia itself is a visible current. Almodóvar’s “Broken Embraces,” Tarantino’s “Inglourious Basterds,” Tsai’s “Face” and Gilliam’s “Parnassus” all seem likely to foreground performance, fantasy, genre, image-making or the legacy of cinema. Cannes, as always, is not just showing films; it is celebrating cinema’s own mythology.

---

## Cannes as Marketplace: The Marché du Film

Beyond the red carpet and critical speculation, Cannes remains the world’s most important film marketplace. The **Marché du Film** runs alongside the festival and functions as a vast global trading floor where producers, sales agents, distributors, financiers, broadcasters and festival programmers buy, sell and package films.

In 2009, this marketplace role is especially important because the film industry is navigating the effects of the global financial crisis. Credit is tighter, specialty distributors are more cautious, and independent film financing has become more difficult. Cannes therefore serves not only as a prestige launchpad but as a practical business environment where projects seek survival.

For finished films, a Cannes premiere can determine international distribution prospects. A strong Competition reception can transform a difficult art-house title into a must-buy property. A major award can create months of sales momentum. Even critical controversy can help certain films stand out in a crowded marketplace.

For unfinished projects, Cannes is where financing conversations happen in hotel suites, private screenings, beach pavilions and hurried meetings along the Croisette. Producers arrive with scripts, cast attachments, promo reels and gap-financing needs. Sales companies test buyer appetite territory by territory. Distributors look for films that can fill release slates over the next year. The glamour is real, but it is also a sales mechanism.

The festival’s hierarchy matters commercially. A Competition slot carries the most prestige, but Un Certain Regard, Directors’ Fortnight, Critics’ Week, midnight screenings and out-of-competition premieres can all influence a film’s international value. Cannes is one of the few places where artistic reputation, media heat and business negotiation converge instantly.

---

## What Is at Stake in 2009?

Cannes 2009 has the feel of a festival trying to balance several identities at once.

It is a temple of the auteur, welcoming back Haneke, Almodóvar, Resnais, Loach, Campion, von Trier and Tarantino. It is a showcase for global cinema, with major entries from France, Spain, Germany, Britain, Italy, South Korea, China, Taiwan, Hong Kong, the Philippines and Palestine. It is a Hollywood platform, opening with Pixar and welcoming Brad Pitt, Ang Lee, Terry Gilliam and Sam Raimi. And it is a business engine, helping the international industry navigate a difficult economic moment.

The biggest question is whether the Competition will produce a consensus masterpiece or a field of divisive provocations. On paper, **“The White Ribbon,” “A Prophet,” “Broken Embraces,” “Bright Star,” “Antichrist,” “Thirst”** and **“Inglourious Basterds”** all have the potential to dominate discussion. But Cannes is famous for surprises: a film that looks minor can emerge as a revelation, while the most anticipated titles can split the press corps.

What seems certain is that Cannes 2009 will not be quiet. With Tarantino back in town, von Trier preparing to provoke, Pixar opening the festival, Gilliam unveiling Heath Ledger’s final performance, and a Competition stacked with world-class filmmakers, this edition promises a rich mix of artistry, argument, commerce and spectacle.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a journalistic overview of the 2009 Cannes Film Festival opening night, with background on key films, directors, economic pressures on media coverage and parties, and expert commentary from Leah Rozen and Jay Weissberg.
counterfactuals.output:
The 2009 Cannes Film Festival opened on May 13 under the unusual glow of 3-D glasses, recession anxiety and a flying house. Pixar’s **“Up,”** directed by **Pete Docter** and co-directed by **Bob Peterson**, became the first animated feature — and the first 3-D film — to open the festival, giving Cannes a populist, family-friendly curtain-raiser at a moment when much of the global film business was bracing for contraction.

The choice was symbolically rich. Cannes has long balanced auteur prestige with industry spectacle, but “Up” represented a new kind of opening-night statement: animation treated not as a sidebar novelty but as a major cinematic event. The film, about an elderly widower who escapes grief by lifting his home into the sky with balloons, arrived with Pixar’s reputation at its height after “WALL-E” and “Ratatouille.” Its emotional weight and technical polish made it a warmer-than-usual opener for a festival better known for provocation, politics and art-house difficulty.

Yet the mood on the Croisette was not simply celebratory. The **global financial crisis** had sharply affected the ecosystem around Cannes. News organizations sent smaller teams; freelancers faced tighter commissioning budgets; luxury brands and distributors scaled back entertainment spending. The festival’s famous parties, yacht gatherings and beachfront promotional events were still present, but many were leaner, more controlled and less extravagant than in the boom years. The glamour remained, but it was harder to ignore the cost of producing it.

The competition lineup, however, suggested that Cannes was not retreating creatively. Among the most anticipated titles was **Quentin Tarantino’s “Inglourious Basterds,”** a World War II revenge fantasy starring Brad Pitt and Christoph Waltz. Tarantino’s return to Cannes carried historical resonance: “Pulp Fiction” had won the Palme d’Or in 1994, and his premieres on the Croisette had become events in themselves.

Also looming was **Lars von Trier’s “Antichrist,”** starring Charlotte Gainsbourg and Willem Dafoe, which would become one of the most divisive films of the festival. Von Trier, already a Cannes lightning rod after films such as “Breaking the Waves” and “Dancer in the Dark,” brought a work of grief, violence and psychological extremity that seemed almost designed to split critics.

Spanish auteur **Pedro Almodóvar** arrived with **“Broken Embraces,”** reuniting with Penélope Cruz in a noir-inflected melodrama about cinema, identity and obsession. **Jane Campion**, the only woman to have won the Palme d’Or outright at that point, presented **“Bright Star,”** her restrained and lyrical account of the romance between poet John Keats and Fanny Brawne. **Ang Lee** brought **“Taking Woodstock,”** a gentler period piece about the cultural mythology surrounding the 1969 music festival. Other major names included **Andrea Arnold** with **“Fish Tank,”** **Gaspar Noé** with **“Enter the Void,”** and **Michael Haneke** with **“The White Ribbon,”** which would go on to win the Palme d’Or.

The festival jury was led by French actress **Isabelle Huppert**, a Cannes icon whose presence reinforced the festival’s commitment to serious, demanding cinema. Her jury would ultimately favor Haneke’s austere black-and-white drama, but on opening night the awards race was still fluid, with speculation focused on the established auteurs and the possibility of a surprise breakthrough.

Commentators at the time noted the tension between Cannes as an artistic institution and Cannes as a luxury marketplace. Film journalist **Leah Rozen**, known for her coverage of Hollywood and festival culture, observed in effect that the festival’s mythology depended on excess — red carpets, stars, parties and press attention — even as media outlets and studios were under pressure to justify every expense. The result was a Cannes that still looked glamorous from the outside but felt more cautious behind the scenes.

**Jay Weissberg** of *Variety*, a longtime international critic, approached the festival from the perspective of cinema’s global marketplace. His commentary emphasized that Cannes remained indispensable because it concentrated prestige, criticism, distribution and international visibility in one place. Even in a downturn, a strong Cannes reception could transform a film’s prospects, especially for foreign-language and auteur-driven work that depended on festival validation to travel.

Opening night therefore carried a double message. With “Up,” Cannes embraced technological change, animation and emotional accessibility. With the broader lineup, it reaffirmed its allegiance to difficult, director-led cinema. And with the recession shadowing every hotel booking, press pass and party invitation, the 2009 festival revealed how vulnerable even the world’s most prestigious film gathering was to economic forces beyond the red carpet.

The balloons of “Up” may have lifted the opening-night crowd, but the festival itself was navigating heavier weather: a changing media business, a strained luxury economy and a film industry searching for proof that artistry and spectacle could still command the world’s attention.
